<result>I have thorough coverage across all six requested areas. Here is the research report.

## 1. First-run / onboarding flags — none exist today

`macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/DefaultsKeys.swift` (the single `Defaults.Keys` extension, lines 27-225) has no `isFirstRun`/`hasCompletedOnboarding`/`hasSeenWelcome` key of any kind. The closest analog is:

- `Defaults.Keys.lastSeenVersion` (`DefaultsKeys.swift:186-189`, `Key<String?>("app.lastSeenVersion", default: nil)`) — drives the "What's New" dialog.
- `WhatsNewService.checkOnLaunch()` (`macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/WhatsNewService.swift:40-63`) explicitly treats `nil` as "fresh install / first launch after this feature shipped: record, no backfill" and **deliberately suppresses** the dialog on a brand-new install (line 47-49: `Defaults[.lastSeenVersion] = currentStr; return nil`). This is the one place in the codebase that already distinguishes "never launched before" from "upgraded," and it's the natural sibling for a new `hasCompletedOnboarding`/`onboardingSeenVersion` key — issue #151 will need to add its own key rather than overload this one (their semantics differ: this one is "don't show release notes on day one," an onboarding flag is "do show something on day one").

There is a **documented gotcha directly relevant to any new Defaults flag**: `macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/UITestFixture.swift:490-527` — a plain launch-argument (e.g. `-hasSeenOnboarding 1`) arrives in the **argument domain**, which outranks the app's persisted domain and is read as a **string**, not a bool. A typed `Defaults[...]` read does `as? Bool` and silently falls back to the key's default, which then **also shadows every later write** for the rest of that process's life. Any test/dev harness for an onboarding flag must mirror the `UITestFixture` pattern (a UserDefaults `bool(forKey:)` coercion, or a fixture-namespaced arg mirrored into `Defaults` before first read) rather than relying on a bare launch arg.

## 2. Empty-project-list state — already exists

`macapp/WorkroomApp/Views/ProjectSidebar.swift:96-110`:

```swift
if store.projects.isEmpty {
  ContentUnavailableView {
    Label("No projects yet", systemImage: "folder.badge.plus")
  } description: {
    Text("Add a Git or Jujutsu project folder to start managing its workrooms.")
  } actions: {
    Button("Add Project…") { store.requestAddProject = true }
      .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
  }
} else {
  tree
}
```

Standard SwiftUI `ContentUnavailableView`, gated on `store.projects.isEmpty` (also read at `AppStore.swift:2584` in `bootstrap()` to decide whether a fresh window needs to hit the CLI, and at `RootView.swift:441` to disable "New Workroom" (⌘N) via `hasProjects`). This is currently the *entire* first-run visual — no separate "welcome" surface exists; a brand-new install today just shows this sidebar empty state plus a blank detail pane. Any onboarding work either extends this view or replaces/precedes it with a dedicated flow.

## 3. Add-project flow (CLI + app)

**Go CLI** — `cmd/add_project.go`:
- `addProjectCmd` (lines 32-60): hidden, `--json`-only command `add-project [PATH]`, with a `--create` flag (`addProjectCreate`, registered at line 210-211).
- `runAddProjectExisting` (67-86): PATH must already be a detected Git/JJ repo.
- `runAddProjectCreate` (109-188): full decision tree in the doc comment (109-108) — creates+`git init`s an empty/non-existent directory, rejects a non-empty non-repo directory (`ErrUnsupportedVCS`), rolls back the created directory on any later failure (154-158).

**macOS app**:
- `Views/AddProjectSheet.swift` — the "New Project" dialog (issue #103). `AddProjectMode` (existing vs createNew, lines 7-11), `AddProjectSheetModel` (pure, unit-tested path normalization/validation/footer text, 16-54), and the sheet UI itself (64-147) with a `Picker("Source")` between "From existing path…" and "Create new directory…" (98-99), a path `TextField` + `Choose…` folder-picker (`fileImporter`, 139-145).
- `Core/AppStore.swift:2983-2999` — `addProject(_:create:)` calls `cli.addProject`, reloads, then **selects the new project and opens a terminal on its root** rather than leaving it on the "nothing selected" state (comment references issue #104 at line 2990).
- Wiring: `AppStore.swift:592` (`@Published var requestAddProject = false`) is the trigger both the sidebar's empty-state button and a menu command set; `RootView.swift:27, 197-200` owns the actual `@State private var showAddProject` sheet presentation via `.onChange(of: store.requestAddProject)`.
- Tests: `WorkroomAppTests/AddProjectSheetModelTests.swift`, `WorkroomAppTests/AppStoreAddProjectTests.swift`.

This flow is already a strong candidate to be the "primary action" inside a first-run welcome screen (reuse `AddProjectSheet`/`store.requestAddProject` rather than building a parallel picker).

## 4. Auxiliary window / Scene patterns

`macapp/WorkroomApp/WorkroomApp.swift:57-88` — the entire `Scene` body:
- `WindowGroup(for: WindowSeed.self)` (62-68) — value-based per-window scene (issue #70), one fresh `AppStore` per window, `RootWindow(seed:)`.
- `Settings { SettingsView() ... }` (77-82) — the **only** other Scene. There is **no separate About window/Scene** — About is a *pane inside Settings* (`SettingsPane.about`, `Core/SettingsPane.swift:21,32,43`), rendered by `Views/SettingsView.swift:202+` ("About + updates (issue #91)").
- No `MenuBarExtra` Scene either — the menu-bar item is hand-rolled AppKit (`MenuBarController`, comment at `WorkroomApp.swift:84-87`) specifically because `MenuBarExtra` gives no hook to intercept a click with nothing pending.

Gotchas for a **new auxiliary window** (documented across `AppDelegate`/`WindowRegistry`):
- `WorkroomApp.swift:220,238`: "Settings, About, Sparkle's updater or the quick terminal" are all windows with **no `AppStore`** — every `shortcutStore`/`switcherGate` lookup treats them as unregistered, so app-wide shortcuts just no-op there rather than needing an allowlist.
- `WorkroomApp.swift:310-320`: ⌘W on an auxiliary window (Settings, About) has no menu-bound "Close Terminal" to fall back on, so a local key-monitor branch explicitly calls `keyWindow.performClose(nil)` for any window with `WindowRegistry.shared.store(for:) == nil`.
- `Core/WindowRegistry.swift:71`: "Settings/About/quick terminal closing here is a no-op" — the registry only tracks workroom windows; an onboarding window would need the same non-registration treatment (or explicit registration if it should influence `lastActiveStore`/quit behavior).
- `WindowRegistry.swift:165`: cycling logic (⌘`) works "front-to-back z-order" across Settings/About panels too.

**Implication for #151**: a dedicated onboarding window is architecturally closest to `Settings` (a small `Scene` with no `AppStore`) — but the existing precedent (`WhatsNewSheet`, see §5 below) is to present it as a **sheet on the launch `RootWindow`** rather than mint a new `Scene`, which sidesteps all the aux-window shortcut/registry carve-outs above.

## 5. App entry point / launch hook point

- `macapp/WorkroomApp/main.swift` — real entry point (no `@main`); dispatches to Ghostty's CLI action handler when invoked as `ghostty`, otherwise calls `WorkroomApp.main()`.
- `WorkroomApp.swift:9-55` (`struct WorkroomApp: App`, `init()`) — Sentry start, PATH `setenv`, `ShellEnvironment.refresh()` detached task, `UITestFixture.applyFixtureDefaults()`. Runs before any window exists.
- `WorkroomApp.swift:185-266`, `AppDelegate.applicationDidFinishLaunching` — window tabbing disabled, notification delegate wired, `MenuBarController` created, `SwitcherPanelController` prepared, `resignActiveObserver` installed. This is the AppKit-level launch hook, but it fires before any `AppStore`/window exists, so it's not where a *first-run UI* would be shown — only where a first-run *side effect* (e.g., seeding something) would go.
- **The actual pattern to copy for showing UI on first run is `RootView.rootLifecycle`** (`Views/RootView.swift:347-378`): a `.task { guard store.isRestoreWindow else { return }; ... }` gated on `AppStore.isRestoreWindow` (`AppStore.swift:142`), feeding a `@State private var whatsNewContent: WhatsNewSheetContent?` and `.sheet(item:)`. This guarantees the check/dialog fires exactly once (only on the launch/restore window, never on a `⌘N` sibling). An onboarding sheet would plug into this exact same `.task`/`.sheet(item:)` slot, gated on the new "has completed onboarding" Default instead of `whatsNew.checkOnLaunch()`.

## 6. Theme / design-token system

`macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/`:
- `Theme.swift` (67 lines) — theme model basics.
- `ThemeService.swift` (387 lines) — resolves the active theme family/variant from `Defaults[.theme]` / `Defaults[.themeFamily]` (`DefaultsKeys.swift:30,35`), applies it app-wide, exposed via `@Environment(ThemeService.self)`.
- `ThemeTokens.swift` (331 lines) — the actual design-token struct (`ThemeTokens`, lines 16+): `bg/fg/panel/fgMuted/fgDim/surface/border/hover/tabActive/accent/accentSoft/warning/failure/conflict/diffAdd·RemoveFg/syntaxByCategory` etc., all derived once per theme change (comment at line 4-15 notes the fallback path: "first launch before a theme is applied … degrades to the pre-theming native look rather than crashing" — i.e., the token system already anticipates a pre-theme-resolution moment, which is exactly the state a first-run window would render in before any project/theme context exists).
- `Views/ThemePicker.swift` — the UI for picking a theme family, useful reference for how theme-aware chrome is composed in this app.

**Any onboarding screen should read `ThemeTokens` via `@Environment(ThemeService.self).tokens` (as every other view does) rather than hardcoding colors** — consistent with `WhatsNewSheet.swift` and `SettingsView.swift`, both of which are the closest existing "polished modal content" precedents to model a welcome screen's visual language on.

---

**Summary for planning #151**: nothing bespoke exists yet — no `isFirstRun` flag, no welcome window, no onboarding Scene. But three strong, reusable seams already exist: (a) the `ProjectSidebar` empty state (`ContentUnavailableView` + `store.requestAddProject`) as the fallback/anchor once onboarding dismisses, (b) `AddProjectSheet` as the ready-made "get your first project in" step, and (c) the `WhatsNewService`/`RootView.rootLifecycle` `.task` + `.sheet(item:)` pattern (gated on `store.isRestoreWindow`) as the exact wiring template for presenting a first-run experience exactly once, on the correct window, styled through `ThemeTokens`.</result>

input.prompt:
Repo: /Users/joelmoss/dev/workroom. Read macapp/CLAUDE.md first. This is planning-only — produce a detailed implementation plan, do not write any code.

## Task
GitHub issue #151 (joelmoss/workroom): "New install setup — Need a great looking startup intro and flow for first time usage." The issue body is that single sentence, no further spec — scope has been decided via user Q&A (below). Design the concrete implementation.

## Decisions already made by the user (do not re-litigate these)
1. **Wizard, not a single sheet.** Steps: Welcome → Feature tour → Add Project → Done (4 steps).
2. **Trigger**: first launch ever, only if zero projects are registered. One-shot — a new persisted flag (e.g. `Defaults.Keys.hasCompletedOnboarding`), following the same "nil/never-seen = first launch" pattern `WhatsNewService` uses for `lastSeenVersion` (`macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/WhatsNewService.swift:40-63`, `DefaultsKeys.swift:186-189`). If the user relaunches without finishing the wizard, it should still show again (not yet marked complete) — but once marked complete (or once a project exists), never show again.
3. **Presentation**: a **dedicated onboarding window/Scene** (like `Settings { SettingsView() }` in `macapp/WorkroomApp/WorkroomApp.swift:77-82`), NOT a sheet over `RootWindow`. This means it needs its own handling for the aux-window gotchas found in research (see below) — no `AppStore` for shortcut/switcher lookups, no menu-bound close item so `⌘W` needs the `WindowRegistry.shared.store(for:) == nil` fallback path, front-to-back cycling inclusion, etc.

## Research already done (treat as ground truth, verify by reading the files before finalizing)
- No existing onboarding/first-run flag or window exists anywhere in macapp.
- `ProjectSidebar.swift:96-110` — existing empty-project-list `ContentUnavailableView`, gated on `store.projects.isEmpty`, with an "Add Project…" button setting `store.requestAddProject = true`. This stays as-is (fallback for anyone who dismisses/skips the wizard); the wizard's "Add Project" step should ideally drive the same underlying logic (`AppStore.addProject(_:create:)` at `AppStore.swift:2983-2999`, and/or reuse `AddProjectSheetModel`'s validation logic from `Views/AddProjectSheet.swift:16-54`) rather than duplicating path-validation code.
- CLI backing: `cmd/add_project.go` — `add-project [PATH] --create` (Go), decision tree at lines 109-188 (creates+git-inits, rejects non-empty non-repo dirs, rolls back on failure).
- Scene body: `macapp/WorkroomApp/WorkroomApp.swift:57-88`. Only two Scenes exist today: `WindowGroup(for: WindowSeed.self)` (62-68, per-window `AppStore`, issue #70) and `Settings { ... }` (77-82, no `AppStore`). No `MenuBarExtra` (hand-rolled AppKit `MenuBarController` instead, comment at 84-87 explains why).
- Aux-window gotchas to replicate for a new onboarding Scene (all currently written for Settings/About, which share "no AppStore"):
  - `WorkroomApp.swift:220,238` — shortcut/switcher lookups treat windows with no registered `AppStore` as no-ops, no allowlist needed.
  - `WorkroomApp.swift:310-320` — local key-monitor ⌘W fallback: `if WindowRegistry.shared.store(for: keyWindow) == nil { keyWindow.performClose(nil) }`.
  - `Core/WindowRegistry.swift:71` — Settings/About closing is a no-op in the registry (not tracked); decide whether onboarding needs the same treatment or explicit registration (probably same treatment, since it's transient and shouldn't affect `lastActiveStore`/quit-dialog logic — check `macapp/CLAUDE.md`'s "Quit dialog reflects dev servers still stop with persistent sessions" recent commit `9a5d10da` for how quit/window-counting logic works, to make sure a stray onboarding window doesn't confuse "should we show a quit confirmation" logic).
  - `WindowRegistry.swift:165` — front-to-back ⌘` cycling already includes Settings/About; onboarding should too by default (no special-casing needed if it follows the same non-registration pattern).
- Launch hook precedent (for reference/pattern, even though presentation differs): `RootView.swift:347-378`, `rootLifecycle` — `.task { guard store.isRestoreWindow else { return }; ... }` gated on `AppStore.isRestoreWindow` (`AppStore.swift:142`), used by `WhatsNewService.checkOnLaunch()`. For a **separate window** instead of a sheet, the equivalent gate needs to live where the app decides which window(s) to open at launch — investigate `AppDelegate.applicationDidFinishLaunching` (`WorkroomApp.swift:185-266`) and how the initial `WindowGroup(for: WindowSeed.self)` window gets its first `WindowSeed` (restore-window creation path) to find the right place to open the onboarding Scene's window instead of / in addition to the normal first window when the new flag says "show onboarding."
- Dev-harness gotcha: `UITestFixture.swift:490-527` documents that a bare launch argument for a Defaults-backed bool is read from the argument domain as a **string** and silently shadows the real default and all later writes. Any new `hasCompletedOnboarding` fixture flag for UI tests must follow `UITestFixture`'s existing mirroring pattern, not a bare `-flag 1` arg.
- Theming: every polished modal in this app (`WhatsNewSheet`, `SettingsView`) reads `@Environment(ThemeService.self).tokens` (`Core/ThemeTokens.swift`) rather than hardcoding colors; the onboarding window must do the same. Note `ThemeTokens.swift:4-15`'s documented fallback for "first launch before a theme is applied" — the onboarding window may render before theme resolution completes, so check how `ThemeService`/`ThemeTokens` initializes and whether the onboarding window needs to wait for it or already degrades gracefully.
- "Feature tour" step: no existing carousel/pager component was found in the codebase in the initial research pass — check whether one exists (search for `TabView(.page` or similar paging patterns) before assuming it needs to be built from scratch. Content for the 3-4 feature highlights should be informed by what the app's core marketed features actually are — check `macapp/CLAUDE.md` and the root `CLAUDE.md` for the app's positioning (workrooms via git worktrees/JJ workspaces, embedded terminals, project sidebar) to write real, accurate highlight copy rather than generic placeholder text.

## What the plan must cover
1. New Defaults key(s) and where declared (`DefaultsKeys.swift` pattern).
2. Where the "should I show onboarding" decision is made and where the new Scene/window gets opened at launch (exact hook point in `AppDelegate`/`WorkroomApp.swift`), including interaction with existing restore-window / multi-window logic — must not show onboarding on every new window (⌘N), only once at app launch.
3. The new Scene definition and its root view hierarchy: a step-based wizard (Welcome / Feature tour / Add Project / Done), what SwiftUI state machine/enum drives step navigation, and window sizing/chrome (fixed size vs resizable — look at how `SettingsView`/`WhatsNewSheet` size themselves for precedent).
4. How the "Add Project" step reuses existing validation/creation logic (`AddProjectSheetModel`, `AppStore.addProject`) rather than forking it — name the exact functions to call or refactor into a shared helper if the current code is too tightly coupled to `AddProjectSheet`'s sheet-specific state.
5. How completion is recorded (when exactly `hasCompletedOnboarding` flips: on reaching "Done", on adding a project, on explicit skip — decide based on decision #2's "still show again if not finished" requirement) and how the window closes/hands off to the normal app window afterward.
6. Aux-window integration: `WindowRegistry`, ⌘W fallback, shortcut/switcher no-op treatment, quit-dialog/window-counting interaction (per commit `9a5d10da`'s logic) — confirm the onboarding window is excluded the same way Settings/About are, or explain why it needs different treatment.
7. UI-test fixture plan for the new Defaults flag, following `UITestFixture`'s existing mirroring pattern (see gotcha above) — needed so XCUITest can force-show or force-skip onboarding deterministically.
8. Feature-tour content and pager mechanism — reuse existing paging UI if found, else specify what minimal SwiftUI construct to use (e.g. native `TabView(selection:).tabViewStyle(.page)` — check macOS availability/behavior since `.page` style is primarily iOS; may need a custom simple step-dot indicator instead).
9. Visual design direction using `ThemeTokens` — reference `WhatsNewSheet.swift`/`SettingsView.swift` as the existing "polished modal content" precedent to model spacing/typography/token usage on, so it reads as "great looking" per the issue title, not generic.
10. Testing/verification plan: unit tests for any new pure logic (mirroring `AddProjectSheetModelTests.swift`/`AppStoreAddProjectTests.swift` patterns), and how to manually verify end-to-end via a throwaway `$HOME` (per the `qa-isolated-home-not-real-config` memory pattern — isolate `~/.config/workroom` AND note that `Defaults`-backed state like a new onboarding flag is NOT isolated by `$HOME` alone, per the `userdefaults-not-isolated-by-home` memory — so manual verification needs a separate bundle-ID-scoped defaults wipe, not just a throwaway HOME).

Read the actual files (`WorkroomApp.swift`, `AppStore.swift` around `isRestoreWindow`/window-open logic, `WindowRegistry.swift`, `DefaultsKeys.swift`, `AddProjectSheet.swift`, `ThemeTokens.swift`, `ProjectSidebar.swift`) to verify all of the above line numbers and confirm/correct the research before finalizing. Return a concrete, file-by-file implementation plan with function/type names to add or modify, not prose-level generalities.

## Corrections to the supplied research (verified by reading the files)

1. **⌘` cycling does NOT include Settings/About today, and onboarding should follow that same exclusion — not be specially added.** `WindowRegistry.isCycleableWindow` (`macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/WindowRegistry.swift:181-184`) requires `store(for: window) != nil || window is QuickTerminalWindow`. Its own doc comment (`WindowRegistry.swift:163-167`) says the cycle is workroom windows *plus the quick terminal*, "deliberately not the Settings / About panels." So leaving the onboarding window unregistered (see below) correctly *excludes* it from ⌘` cycling, matching precedent — this needs zero new code, but it's an exclusion, not an inclusion.

2. **Theming precedent is not `@Environment(ThemeService.self)`.** No view in the app uses that. `WhatsNewSheet.swift:19` and `SettingsView.swift` both do `private let theme = ThemeService.shared` (it's `@MainActor @Observable`, `ThemeService.swift:30-31`) and read `theme.tokens.*`/`ThemeService.shared.tokens.*` directly in `body`. The `ThemeTokens.swift:9` doc comment claiming `@Environment` usage is aspirational/incorrect — nothing reads it that way. The onboarding window should copy the actual pattern.

3. **Theme readiness is a non-issue.** `ThemeService.init()` (`ThemeService.swift:148-151`) computes `tokens` synchronously from `Defaults[.themeFamily]` before any window can render — there's no async gap to guard against. The "first launch before a theme is applied" comment in `ThemeTokens.swift` is about a *missing/invalid theme file* fallback, not a load race.

## Key design decision (diverges from the literal research prompt — resolved via advisor review)

The research suggested giving the onboarding window "no `AppStore`" like Settings. That's right for *window registration* (never call `WindowRegistry.shared.register(window:store:)` for it — see §6), but the wizard's Add-Project step still needs to *mutate* the real project list, and `AppStore.addProject` does more than register a path: after `reload()` it sets `selectedProjectID`/`selectedTargetID = .root(project:)` (issue #104 — land the user on the new project instead of "Nothing selected"). Constructing a throwaway `AppStore(projectStore: .shared)` just for the wizard would call that tail on an object nobody's looking at, so the real (launch) window's sidebar would show the new project with nothing selected — a visible regression versus what `AddProjectSheet` already does today.

**Fix:** the wizard drives the *existing, visible* launch-window store: `WindowRegistry.shared.lastActiveStore`. This is an established, documented seam — `AppDelegate.shortcutStore`'s doc comment (`WorkroomApp.swift:216-224`) and `lastActiveStore`'s own doc comment (`WindowRegistry.swift:39-41`, "modal-safe... a quit alert / Settings / About becoming key never changes it") both establish that a foreign/unregistered window becoming key doesn't disturb it, and by construction the launch `RootWindow` is registered (and hence `lastActiveStore` is non-nil) well before the wizard's Add-Project step can be interacted with (registration happens in `WindowAccessor`'s `viewDidMoveToWindow`, ahead of the `.task` that opens the onboarding window).

## 1. New Defaults key — `macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/DefaultsKeys.swift`

Add, alongside `lastSeenVersion` (same "unset = first launch" shape):

```swift
/// Whether the first-launch onboarding wizard (issue #151) has been completed. False on a fresh
/// install — following the same "unset/false = first launch" pattern as `lastSeenVersion`. Flips
/// to true when the wizard reaches its last step, or when a project is added from inside it
/// (`OnboardingWindow`); the wizard is gated on this AND an empty project list
/// (`OnboardingGate.shouldShow`), so completing it — or adding a project some other way before ever
/// opening it — means it never shows again, but closing the window early leaves this false, so it
/// shows again next launch.
static let hasCompletedOnboarding = Key<Bool>("onboarding.hasCompleted", default: false)
```

Deliberately **not** written from inside `AppStore.addProject` itself — that function has an existing test file (`AppStoreAddProjectTests.swift`) and a second caller (`ProjectSidebar`'s plain "Add Project…" fallback) that has nothing to do with onboarding. Since the show-gate already checks `projects.isEmpty`, a project existing is sufficient on its own to suppress onboarding; welding a `Defaults` write into the shared mutation path only buys the rare "user deletes their only project later" case, which nobody asked for. The flag is set only from the onboarding view itself (§5).

**Scene declaration** — add a new single-instance `Window` scene (macOS 13+, fine at this app's macOS 15+ floor), placed after the `WindowGroup(for: WindowSeed.self)` block (only the *first* declared scene auto-opens at launch, so ordering here matters — put it next to `Settings`, not before the `WindowGroup`):

```swift

  OnboardingWindow()
}

Settings {
  SettingsView()
    ...
}
```

No `.commands { ... }` on it (Settings has none either — the app-wide `WorkroomCommands` from the `WindowGroup` scene already covers the menu bar) and no `.environmentObject` injections — the view needs none (see §5).

**Launch hook** — in `RootWindow.body`'s existing `.task` (`WorkroomApp.swift:155-174`), right after bootstrap resolves and the existing `guard seed.isLaunch else { return }`:

```swift

  guard ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["XCTestConfigurationFilePath"] == nil else { return }
  await store.bootstrap(restore: seed.restore)
  guard seed.isLaunch else { return }
  if OnboardingGate.shouldShow(
    hasCompleted: Defaults[.hasCompletedOnboarding], projectsEmpty: store.projects.isEmpty
  ) {
    openWindow(id: OnboardingWindow.sceneID)
  }
  for key in ProjectStore.shared.pendingSessionKeys() {

```

This reuses the `@Environment(\.openWindow) private var openWindow` already declared on `RootWindow` (`WorkroomApp.swift:122`). Gating on `seed.isLaunch` is what stops onboarding from ever considering itself on a ⌘N window (only the launch window's `.task` runs this branch at all — restored siblings return before reaching it, exactly like the What's-New check and the session fan-out already do). `openWindow(id:)` on a `Window` (not `WindowGroup`) scene is idempotent if called twice — no double-open risk from a `.task` re-fire, same reasoning already documented for the sibling-restore loop right below it.

enum OnboardingStep: Int, CaseIterable {
  case welcome, tour, addProject, done

/// Pure decision logic for whether the wizard should open, extracted so it's unit-testable without
/// a window (mirrors `AddProjectSheetModel`). Trigger: first launch ever, only while no project is
/// registered. `override` lets a UI test force either outcome deterministically — see
/// `UITestFixture.onboardingOverride`; defaults to that real flag in production, injected explicitly
/// in tests.
enum OnboardingGate {
  static func shouldShow(
    hasCompleted: Bool, projectsEmpty: Bool, override: Bool? = UITestFixture.onboardingOverride
  ) -> Bool {
    if let override { return override }
    return !hasCompleted && projectsEmpty
  }
}

/// The dedicated first-run onboarding window (issue #151) — a `Window` scene (WorkroomApp.swift),
/// not a sheet over RootWindow. Deliberately carries NO `WindowAccessor`/`WindowRegistry.register`:
/// staying unregistered is what makes it fall through the same "no AppStore" paths Settings/About
/// already use — the ⌘W fallback (AppDelegate's key monitor), the shortcut/switcher no-ops
/// (`AppDelegate.shortcutStore`/`switcherGate`), the quit/window-count logic (`WindowRegistry
/// .allStores`), and the ⌘` cycle exclusion (`isCycleableWindow`) all come out right for free.
struct OnboardingWindow: View {
  static let sceneID = "onboarding"

  @Environment(\.dismissWindow) private var dismissWindow
  @State private var step: OnboardingStep = .welcome
  private let theme = ThemeService.shared

  var body: some View {
    VStack(spacing: 0) {
      content.frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity)
      Divider()
      footer
    }
    .frame(width: 560, height: 480)
    .background(theme.tokens.panel.ignoresSafeArea())
    .accessibilityIdentifier("onboarding.window")
  }

  @ViewBuilder private var content: some View {
    switch step {
    case .welcome: OnboardingWelcomeStep()
    case .tour: OnboardingTourStep()
    case .addProject:
      // Reused verbatim (not rebuilt) — same validation, same "Choose…" picker, same copy already
      // covered by AddProjectSheetModelTests. Its own Cancel button doubles as "skip this step."
      AddProjectSheet(
        onAdd: { path, create in Task { await handleAdd(path, create: create) } },
        onCancel: { step = .done })
    case .done:
      OnboardingDoneStep(onFinish: finish)
    }
  }

  private var footer: some View {
    HStack {
      if step != .welcome, step != .addProject {
        Button("Back") { step = OnboardingStep(rawValue: step.rawValue - 1) ?? .welcome }
      }
      Spacer()
      stepDots
      Spacer()
      if step == .welcome || step == .tour {
        Button("Next") { step = OnboardingStep(rawValue: step.rawValue + 1) ?? .done }
          .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
      }
      // .addProject's own buttons drive its advance; .done's button is inside OnboardingDoneStep.
    }
    .padding(16)
  }

  private var stepDots: some View {
    HStack(spacing: 6) {
      ForEach(OnboardingStep.allCases, id: \.self) { s in
        Circle().fill(s == step ? theme.tokens.accent : theme.tokens.fgDim)
          .frame(width: 6, height: 6)
      }
    }
  }

  /// §4: routes through the existing launch window's store rather than a throwaway one, so a
  /// successful add lands the user on the new project's root exactly as it does from the sidebar
  /// (`AppStore.addProject`'s post-`reload()` selection, issue #104) instead of a silent no-op.
  private func handleAdd(_ path: String, create: Bool) async {
    guard let store = WindowRegistry.shared.lastActiveStore else { return }
    store.errorMessage = nil  // clear any stale error before reading it as this call's outcome
    await store.addProject(path, create: create)
    guard store.errorMessage == nil else { return }  // leave the sheet up so the user can retry
    Defaults[.hasCompletedOnboarding] = true
    step = .done
  }

  private func finish() {
    Defaults[.hasCompletedOnboarding] = true
    dismissWindow(id: Self.sceneID)
  }
}

private struct OnboardingWelcomeStep: View { /* headline + subhead, matches WhatsNewSheet's header spacing/typography */ }
private struct OnboardingTourStep: View { /* ForEach(OnboardingFeature.all) { ... } cards */ }
private struct OnboardingDoneStep: View {
  let onFinish: () -> Void
  var body: some View {
    VStack(spacing: 16) {
      Spacer()
      Text("You're all set").font(.largeTitle.bold())
      Text("Open a project from the sidebar whenever you're ready.")
        .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
      Spacer()
      Button("Get Started", action: onFinish)
        .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
        .keyboardShortcut(.defaultAction)
    }
    .padding(32)
  }
}

## 5. Completion recording — summarized

- **On "Get Started" (Done step)** → `Defaults[.hasCompletedOnboarding] = true`, then `dismissWindow(id: OnboardingWindow.sceneID)`.
- **On a successful add mid-wizard** → same flag write, inside `handleAdd`, before auto-advancing to `.done` (so the user still sees the Done screen, but the flag is already true — the two writes are simply redundant/idempotent, not conflicting).
- **On close (⌘W, red button, or just walking away) before either of those** → nothing happens; the flag stays `false`, so `OnboardingGate.shouldShow` fires again next launch. No custom `NSWindowDelegate`/close-guard is needed for this — it's the default behavior of doing nothing, which is exactly right per the user's decision ("still show again if not yet finished").
- **Existing fallback stays untouched**: `ProjectSidebar.swift:96-110`'s `ContentUnavailableView` + `store.requestAddProject = true` remains the safety net for anyone who closes the wizard early or on a subsequent still-empty launch before the gate re-fires.

## 6. Aux-window integration — confirmed, no special-casing needed

The single load-bearing implementation rule: **`OnboardingWindow` must never appear inside a `WindowAccessor { WindowRegistry.shared.register(window:store:) }` call** (unlike `RootWindow.body`, `WorkroomApp.swift:149-154`). With that omission:

- **⌘` front-to-back cycling** (`WindowRegistry.isCycleableWindow`, line 181-184): correctly *excludes* the onboarding window, matching the documented Settings/About exclusion — this is the one place the original research had the direction backwards (see §0).

91	/// Identity for a window scene (issue #70). `restore` is true only for the window SwiftUI brings up
92	/// at launch — combined with `ProjectStore.consumeInitialRestore()` that single window reapplies the
93	/// persisted selection; every ⌘N window carries a fresh `restore == false` seed and opens blank.
94	struct WindowSeed: Codable, Hashable {
95	  let id: UUID
96	  /// Whether this window may adopt a saved session — true for the launch window and for each sibling
97	  /// it reopens (issue #46), false for every ⌘N window, which always starts blank.
98	  let restore: Bool
99	  /// Whether this is THE launch window, as opposed to a sibling reopened from the saved session.
100	  ///
101	  /// Separate from `restore` because the two answer different questions and both siblings and the
102	  /// launch window restore. Only the launch window runs the What's-New auto-check and fans the
103	  /// siblings out — without this distinction every restored window would pop that dialog.
104	  var isLaunch = false
105	
106	  /// The launch window: a fresh id allowed to restore the saved session.
107	  static var launch: WindowSeed { WindowSeed(id: UUID(), restore: true, isLaunch: true) }
108	
109	  /// A window reopened from the saved session, keyed on the session it will claim.
110	  static func restoring(key: UUID) -> WindowSeed {
111	    WindowSeed(id: key, restore: true, isLaunch: false)
112	  }
113	}

115	/// One window's root. The value-based `WindowGroup` gives each window its own `RootWindow`, so the
116	/// `@StateObject` below is a fresh per-window `AppStore` sharing the one `ProjectStore`. It injects
117	/// that store into the environment, exposes it to menu commands via `focusedSceneObject`, and
118	/// registers the window↔store pair with `WindowRegistry` (issue #70).
119	struct RootWindow: View {
120	  let seed: WindowSeed
121	  @StateObject private var store: AppStore
122	  @Environment(\.openWindow) private var openWindow
123	
124	  init(seed: WindowSeed) {
125	    self.seed = seed
126	    let store = AppStore(projectStore: .shared)
127	    // Capture the current window's size ONCE, at this window's creation, so the new window can be
128	    // sized to match it before it's shown (issue #70). nil for the launch window.
129	    store.pendingInitialWindowSize = WindowRegistry.shared.preferredNewWindowSize
130	    // Only the launch window runs the What's-New auto-check (see RootView). Sibling windows reopened
131	    // from the saved session also carry `restore: true`, so gating on that would pop the dialog once
132	    // per restored window (issue #46).
133	    store.isRestoreWindow = seed.isLaunch
134	    // Which saved window this one adopts. The launch window takes the first unclaimed session; a
135	    // sibling was opened FOR a specific key and claims exactly that one.
136	    store.sessionKey = seed.id
137	    store.claimsSavedSession = seed.restore
138	    _store = StateObject(wrappedValue: store)
139	  }
140	
141	  var body: some View {
142	    RootView()
143	      .environmentObject(store)
144	      .environmentObject(store.notifications)
145	      .environmentObject(store.terminals)
146	      .environmentObject(store.terminals.agentManager)
147	      .focusedSceneObject(store)
148	      .frame(minWidth: 900, maxWidth: .infinity, minHeight: 560, maxHeight: .infinity)
149	      .background(
150	        WindowAccessor { window in
151	          WindowRegistry.shared.register(window: window, store: store)
152	          store.attachWindow(window)
153	        }
154	      )
155	      .task {
156	        // Not under XCTest: `WorkroomAppTests` hosts this app to get `@testable import Workroom`,
157	        // which means this real WindowGroup scene renders too — and without this guard, its `.task`
158	        // ran on every `make app-test`, unconditionally `bootstrap()`ing the SHARED, non-fake
159	        // `AppStore` (production default `cli: WorkroomCLI.shared`) against the developer's REAL
160	        // `~/.config/workroom/config.json`, then opening a REAL terminal in a REAL project
161	        // directory for whatever it found. Same guard, same reasoning, as the `ShellEnvironment`
162	        // skip in `init` above. Unit tests construct their own isolated `AppStore()`s and never see
163	        // this window at all, so skipping its bootstrap breaks nothing under test.
164	        guard ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["XCTestConfigurationFilePath"] == nil else {
165	          return
166	        }
167	        await store.bootstrap(restore: seed.restore)
168	        // Reopen the windows that were open at the last quit (issue #46). Only the launch window
169	        // fans out, and each key is handed out once, so a `.task` re-fire cannot double-open.
170	        guard seed.isLaunch else { return }
171	        for key in ProjectStore.shared.pendingSessionKeys() {
172	          openWindow(value: WindowSeed.restoring(key: key))
173	        }
174	      }
175	  }
176	}

178	/// Installs the app's local key monitor: the shortcuts that are handled *here* rather than as menu
179	/// items, because they'd clutter the menu (⌘1–9 / ⌥⌘1–9 tab focus), because they have no menu home
180	/// (⌘` window cycling, ⌃⌘arrows pane focus, ⌥Tab / ⌃Tab quick switching), or because the monitor must
181	/// beat a competing menu item (⌘W in the quick terminal). A local monitor runs inside
182	/// `NSApp.sendEvent`, ahead of both menu key-equivalent dispatch and the focused terminal surface, so
183	/// it is also the only place a shortcut can be claimed *conditionally* — see the ⌥Tab / ⌃Tab branch,
184	/// which passes the key back to the terminal when there is nothing to switch to.
185	final class AppDelegate: NSObject, NSApplicationDelegate, UNUserNotificationCenterDelegate {
186	  private var monitor: Any?
187	  /// The global ⌘§ show/hide shortcut while enabled, else nil (issue #13). Registered/torn down by
188	  /// `updateGlobalHotkey()` to follow the `globalHotkey` setting.
189	  private var showHideHotkey: GlobalHotkey?
190	  /// The global ⌥§ quick-terminal shortcut while enabled, else nil (issue #39). Registered/torn down
191	  /// alongside `showHideHotkey` by `updateGlobalHotkey()` under the same `globalHotkey` setting.
192	  private var quickTerminalHotkey: GlobalHotkey?
193	  /// The quick terminal (issue #39) — a ~/ shell in its own chrome-less window. One persistent
194	  /// controller; its window/surface come and go as it's summoned/closed.
195	  private let quickTerminal = QuickTerminalController()
196	  /// Retains the `.showQuickTerminal` observer (posted by the toolbar button) for the app's lifetime.
197	  private var quickTerminalObserver: NSObjectProtocol?
198	  /// Observes the `globalHotkey` setting so toggling it takes effect immediately.
199	  private var hotkeyObservation: Task<Void, Never>?
200	  /// The system menu-bar item (issue #33) — an `NSStatusItem` owned here so a click can branch on the
201	  /// notification count (open the list, or just focus the app when there's nothing pending). Retained
202	  /// for the app's lifetime; created in `applicationDidFinishLaunching`.
203	  private var menuBarController: MenuBarController?
204	  /// Catches SIGTERM so a signalled quit stops run commands gracefully (issue #7). Retained so the
205	  /// `DispatchSource` stays alive for the process's lifetime.
206	  private var sigtermSource: DispatchSourceSignal?
207	  /// Retains the background-save observer (issue #46) for the app's lifetime.
208	  private var resignActiveObserver: Any?
209	
210	  deinit { hotkeyObservation?.cancel() }
211	
212	  /// The store a shortcut in the key monitor below may act on: the one owning the window the event is
213	  /// actually headed for, and only while that window has no command-palette dialog up.
214	  ///
215	  /// Deliberately **not** `WindowRegistry.keyStore`. That resolves
216	  /// `store(for: NSApp.keyWindow) ?? lastActiveStore ?? allStores.first` (WindowRegistry.swift:113),
217	  /// so it falls back *past* a foreign key window — which is right for its other three callers (the
218	  /// menu-bar popover, where `store(for:)` is legitimately nil; notification-click routing; the
219	  /// terminal context menu) but wrong here: it fires ⌘R / ⌘1-9 / ⌥⌘S into a *background* workroom
220	  /// whenever a sheet, Settings, About, Sparkle's updater or the quick terminal is key. Those windows
221	  /// are all unregistered, so `store(for:)` returns nil for them with no extra checks — which is what
222	  /// lets every branch below simply no-op instead of needing a swallow-with-allowlist (an allowlist
223	  /// was the first design; it was the sole source of a ⌘⌫ gap, broken ⌘V on non-Latin layouts, and a
224	  /// ⌘↑/⌘↓ collision with the Scroll to Top/Bottom menu items).
225	  /// `registry` is injectable purely so tests don't have to mutate the `WindowRegistry.shared`
226	  /// singleton — registering on it leaks window registrations into later tests unless every test pairs
227	  /// its cleanup in tearDown. Production always takes the default.
228	  @MainActor static func shortcutStore(
229	    for window: NSWindow?, in registry: WindowRegistry = .shared
230	  ) -> AppStore? {
231	    guard let store = registry.store(for: window), store.activePicker == nil else { return nil }
232	    return store
233	  }
234	
235	  /// What a quick-switcher keystroke (⌥Tab / ⌃Tab, issue #132) should do for `window`.
236	  ///
237	  /// Three outcomes, because this shortcut is the first one whose consumption is *conditional*:
238	  /// - `.passThrough` — not one of our windows (Settings, About, the quick terminal). The key belongs
239	  ///   to whatever is focused there, so ⌃Tab still reaches a TUI in the quick terminal.
240	  /// - `.swallow` — one of ours with a modal up. Raising a window and moving its selection under its
241	  ///   own sheet would leave that sheet acting on a workroom the user never chose (for the commit
242	  ///   sheet, a wrong-target VCS write). Gated on the FULL `hasModalPresentation` predicate, not
243	  ///   `activePicker` — hence resolving through the registry rather than `shortcutStore`, which nils
244	  ///   out a picker window and a foreign window alike, two cases that must differ here.
245	  /// - `.act(store)` — go ahead; whether the event is consumed then depends on whether the switcher
246	  ///   actually switched (nothing to switch to ⇒ the terminal keeps the key).
247	  ///
248	  /// `registry` is injectable for the same reason as `shortcutStore`'s: so tests don't register windows
249	  /// on the shared singleton.
250	  @MainActor static func switcherGate(
251	    for window: NSWindow?, in registry: WindowRegistry = .shared
252	  ) -> SwitcherGate {
253	    guard let store = registry.store(for: window) else { return .passThrough }
254	    return store.hasModalPresentation ? .swallow : .act(store)
255	  }
256	
257	  /// Whether `window` is one of ours *and* has a command-palette dialog open — the case where a
258	  /// shortcut must be actively swallowed rather than merely no-op'd, because the branch doesn't
259	  /// consult a store at all (⌘` window cycling).
260	  @MainActor static func hasModalPicker(
261	    _ window: NSWindow?, in registry: WindowRegistry = .shared
262	  ) -> Bool {
263	    registry.store(for: window)?.activePicker != nil
264	  }

266	  func applicationDidFinishLaunching(_ notification: Notification) {
267	    // Disable native macOS window tabbing. It tabs whole app windows (each with its own
268	    // sidebar) — a level above our per-workroom terminal tabs and a poor fit for a
269	    // single-window, sidebar-driven app. Off, it also drops the auto-injected
270	    // "Show/Hide Tab Bar" + "Show All Tabs" View-menu items that otherwise read as if they
271	    // control the terminal tabs.
272	    NSWindow.allowsAutomaticWindowTabbing = false
273	
274	    // Receive notification clicks (authorization is requested lazily on first post).
275	    UNUserNotificationCenter.current().delegate = self
276	
277	    // Install the menu-bar item (issue #33). Creating it here also forces `WindowRegistry.shared`
278	    // into existence early, so its key-window observer is live before the first window appears.
279	    menuBarController = MenuBarController(registry: .shared)
280	
281	    // Build the switcher rail's panel now, ordered out, and connect it to the session controller
282	    // (issue #132). Pre-created on purpose: the first `NSHostingView` render costs real milliseconds,
283	    // and the 250 ms reveal is the worst possible moment to pay it.
284	    SwitcherPanelController.shared.prepare()
285	    SwitcherPanelController.shared.attach(to: .shared)
286	
287	    // Save the session whenever the app goes to the background (issue #46). Belt and braces on top
288	    // of the coalesced writes: ⌘-tabbing away is the most common moment a user leaves a layout they
289	    // would hate to lose, and it costs nothing when nothing changed (the coordinator compares the
290	    // captured document with the last one written).
291	    resignActiveObserver = NotificationCenter.default.addObserver(
292	      forName: NSApplication.willResignActiveNotification, object: nil, queue: .main
293	    ) { _ in
294	      MainActor.assumeIsolated { SessionCoordinator.shared.writeIfChanged() }
295	    }
296	
297	    monitor = NSEvent.addLocalMonitorForEvents(matching: .keyDown) { event in
298	      let flags = event.modifierFlags.intersection([.command, .shift, .option, .control])
299	      // ⌘W closes the quick terminal (issue #39) when its window is key. The menu's "Close Terminal"
300	      // ⌘W targets the main window's tabs and would otherwise win, so catch it here (like ⌘R / ⌘1–9
301	      // above) and route to the quick-terminal window — its delegate (QuickTerminalController) tears
302	      // the surface down. Gated on the key window being a QuickTerminalWindow, so ⌘W still closes a
303	      // main-window terminal tab everywhere else.
304	      if flags == .command, event.charactersIgnoringModifiers == "w",
305	        let quickTerminalWindow = (event.window ?? NSApp.keyWindow) as? QuickTerminalWindow
306	      {
307	        quickTerminalWindow.performClose(nil)
308	        return nil
309	      }
310	      // ⌘W on an auxiliary window (Settings, About) — a window with no AppStore (not a workroom
311	      // window). The menu's "Close Terminal" owns ⌘W app-wide but is disabled there (no focused
312	      // terminal), so ⌘W would otherwise just beep. Close the window, as the standard File ▸ Close
313	      // would. Workroom windows (store != nil) fall through so their "Close Terminal" still fires.
314	      if flags == .command, event.charactersIgnoringModifiers == "w",
315	        let keyWindow = event.window ?? NSApp.keyWindow,
316	        MainActor.assumeIsolated({ WindowRegistry.shared.store(for: keyWindow) }) == nil
317	      {
318	        keyWindow.performClose(nil)
319	        return nil
320	      }
321	      // The window this event is headed for, resolved once for every branch below. `event.window` is
322	      // nil for ⌘ key-equivalents, hence the `?? NSApp.keyWindow` — same idiom as the two ⌘W branches
323	      // above. Those two run BEFORE this point on purpose: ⌘W acts on the modal in front (a sheet, the
324	      // quick terminal), not on the window behind it, so it must keep working while a dialog is up.
325	      let window = event.window ?? NSApp.keyWindow
326	      // ⌘` / ⇧⌘`: cycle key focus through the app's windows incl. the quick terminal (issue #87) —
327	      // the standard "Move focus to next window" shortcut. Caught here, like ⌘1–9, so the focused
328	      // terminal surface doesn't swallow the backtick as input. keyCode 50 is the grave (`) key,
329	      // matched by code (not char) so it's layout-stable and ⇧⌘` reads as backward despite the "~".
330	      // Consumed regardless (window cycling has no terminal use we want to preserve).
331	      if event.keyCode == 50, flags == .command || flags == [.command, .shift] {
332	        // Alone among the branches here this one consults no store, so `shortcutStore` returning nil
333	        // wouldn't stop it — swallow explicitly while a dialog is up.
334	        if MainActor.assumeIsolated({ Self.hasModalPicker(window) }) { return nil }
335	        let forward = flags == .command
336	        MainActor.assumeIsolated { WindowRegistry.shared.cycleWindows(forward: forward) }
337	        return nil
338	      }
339	      // ⌥Tab / ⌃Tab: the quick switchers (issue #132) — ⌥Tab steps open workrooms across every
340	      // window by most-recent use, ⌃Tab steps the current workroom's panes. Caught here for the same
341	      // reason as ⌘1–9, and *only* here: Tab is deliberately NOT in `isAppShortcut`, because whether
342	      // the app owns it depends on runtime state (a workroom with one pane has nothing to switch to,
343	      // so ⌃Tab must still reach a TUI). Both trigger modifiers are preferences — a global hotkey
344	      // grabber like AltTab beats this monitor and can't be detected.
345	      if QuickSwitcherKey.classify(keyCode: event.keyCode, flags: flags) != nil {
346	        return MainActor.assumeIsolated {
347	          switch Self.switcherGate(for: window) {
348	          case .passThrough: return event
349	          case .swallow: return nil
350	          case .act(let store):
351	            // Autorepeat would spin the switcher (~15 steps/sec); macOS's own ⌘Tab ignores repeats too.
352	            // Tested INSIDE `.act`, not above the gate: above it, a held ⌃Tab in the quick terminal or
353	            // in a single-pane workroom — the cases deliberately handed to the TUI — passed its first
354	            // keystroke through and had every repeat after it silently eaten.
355	            if event.isARepeat { return nil }
356	            guard let hit = QuickSwitcherKey.classify(keyCode: event.keyCode, flags: flags) else {
357	              return event
358	            }
359	            // Consumed only when it switched, so ⌃Tab still reaches a TUI in a single-pane workroom —
360	            // the same rule as the ⌥⌘digit / ⌥⌘arrow branches below.
361	            return QuickSwitcherController.shared.handleTrigger(
362	              hit.kind, reverse: hit.reverse, in: store) ? nil : event
363	          }
364	        }
365	      }
366	      // Escape and ←/→ while a switcher session is live (issue #132). Ahead of every other branch that
367	      // could claim them, because a live session owns the keyboard until it ends — and behind the Tab
368	      // branch above, which is what starts one.
369	      //
370	      // Gated on the window like the Tab branch, and on the modifiers: without the window gate, Escape
371	      // pressed in the quick terminal or in Settings was swallowed to cancel the rail instead of
372	      // dismissing what was actually in front of the user. `handleArrow` enforces the rest — revealed
373	      // only, and no modifier beyond the trigger, so a live session can't steal ⌥⌘←/→ or ⇧⌥⌘←/→.
374	      if MainActor.assumeIsolated({ QuickSwitcherController.shared.isLive }),
375	        MainActor.assumeIsolated({
376	          if case .passThrough = Self.switcherGate(for: window) { false } else { true }
377	        })
378	      {
379	        if event.keyCode == 53 {  // Escape
380	          return MainActor.assumeIsolated { QuickSwitcherController.shared.handleEscape() }
381	            ? nil : event
382	        }
383	        if event.keyCode == 123 || event.keyCode == 124 {  // ← / →
384	          let reverse = event.keyCode == 123

386	            QuickSwitcherController.shared.handleArrow(reverse: reverse, flags: flags)
387	          } ? nil : event
388	        }
389	      }

392	        let digit = Int(chars), (1...9).contains(digit)
393	      {
394	        Task { @MainActor in Self.shortcutStore(for: window)?.focusTerminalTab(at: digit - 1) }
395	        return nil  // consume so it doesn't reach the terminal
396	      }
397	      // ⌥⌘1–9: switch to the Nth workroom tab (issue #23), the workroom-level counterpart to ⌘1–9.
398	      // Caught here (like ⌘1–9) so it fires before the terminal. Consumed only when there's an Nth tab
399	      // to switch to (focusWorkroomTab returns true), so ⌥⌘digit still reaches the terminal otherwise.
400	      // (Digit chars don't collide with the ⌥⌘R / arrow-key checks below.)
401	      if flags == [.command, .option], let chars = event.charactersIgnoringModifiers,
402	        let digit = Int(chars), (1...9).contains(digit),
403	        MainActor.assumeIsolated({
404	          Self.shortcutStore(for: window)?.focusWorkroomTab(at: digit - 1) ?? false
405	        })
406	      {
407	        return nil
408	      }
409	      // ⌘R: run-or-focus the selected workroom's run command (issue #7) — caught here so it fires
410	      // before the terminal swallows it, like ⌘1–9. Consumed unconditionally (⌘R has no terminal use
411	      // we want to preserve); a no-op when nothing's selected, but no command configured now opens the
412	      // Project Settings sheet with a warning instead of doing nothing (issue #127).
413	      if flags == .command, event.charactersIgnoringModifiers?.lowercased() == "r" {
414	        Task { @MainActor in Self.shortcutStore(for: window)?.runOrFocusRunCommand() }
415	        return nil
416	      }
417	      // ⇧⌘R: stop the selected workroom's run command if it's running (issue #7). Caught here (not
418	      // just the menu key-equivalent) so it fires reliably before the terminal, like ⌘R. No-op when
419	      // nothing's running; consumed regardless (it's reserved in `isAppShortcut` anyway).
420	      if flags == [.command, .shift], event.charactersIgnoringModifiers?.lowercased() == "r" {
421	        Task { @MainActor in Self.shortcutStore(for: window)?.stopSelectedRunCommand() }
422	        return nil
423	      }
424	      // ⌥⌘R: restart the selected workroom's run command if it's running (issue #7). Caught here for
425	      // reliability, like ⌘R/⇧⌘R. No-op when nothing's running. (The arrow-key checks below match by
426	      // keyCode, so "r" doesn't collide with tab/pane navigation.)
427	      if flags == [.command, .option], event.charactersIgnoringModifiers?.lowercased() == "r" {
428	        Task { @MainActor in Self.shortcutStore(for: window)?.restartSelectedRunCommand() }
429	        return nil
430	      }
431	      // ⌥⌘←/→: previous/next terminal tab (issue #29). Caught here like ⌘1–9 so it fires before the
432	      // terminal; consumed when it switches a tab, and reserved in `isAppShortcut` anyway so it never
433	      // reaches the terminal as input. (⌥⌘↑/↓ are unbound — they pass through to the terminal.)
434	      if flags == [.command, .option], event.keyCode == 123 || event.keyCode == 124,
435	        MainActor.assumeIsolated({
436	          Self.shortcutStore(for: window)?.cycleTerminalTab(forward: event.keyCode == 124) ?? false
437	        })
438	      {
439	        return nil
440	      }
441	      // ⇧⌥⌘←/→: previous/next workroom tab (issue #29), the workroom-level counterpart to ⌥⌘←/→.
442	      // Consumed when it switches; reserved in `isAppShortcut` anyway, like ⌥⌘←/→.
443	      if flags == [.command, .option, .shift], event.keyCode == 123 || event.keyCode == 124,
444	        MainActor.assumeIsolated({
445	          Self.shortcutStore(for: window)?.cycleWorkroomTab(forward: event.keyCode == 124) ?? false
446	        })
447	      {
448	        return nil
449	      }
450	      // ⌃⌘arrows: move focus between split panes (issue #3) — moved off ⌥⌘arrows, which now cycles
451	      // terminal tabs (issue #29). Consumed only when focus actually moves, so the keys still reach
452	      // the terminal when there's no split to navigate. (Virtual keycodes: left 123 / right 124 /
453	      // down 125 / up 126.)
454	      let arrows: [UInt16: PaneDirection] = [123: .left, 124: .right, 125: .down, 126: .up]
455	      if flags == [.command, .control], let direction = arrows[event.keyCode],
456	        MainActor.assumeIsolated({ Self.shortcutStore(for: window)?.focusPane(direction) ?? false })
457	      {
458	        return nil
459	      }
460	      // ⌃⌘S: toggle the Projects sidebar (issue #128). Caught here — not just left to the menu's
461	      // key-equivalent — so it fires reliably even with a focused TUI (like ⌘1-9 above).
462	      if flags == [.command, .control], event.charactersIgnoringModifiers?.lowercased() == "s" {
463	        Task { @MainActor in Self.shortcutStore(for: window)?.sidebarVisible.toggle() }
464	        return nil
465	      }
466	      // ⌥⌘S: the OS-standard "Toggle Sidebar" shortcut (Finder, Notes, etc. — AppKit's
467	      // `toggleSidebar:` first-responder action). We don't bind it to our own "Projects" menu item

470	      // AppKit auto-wires ITS default toggle to that column regardless of what our menu does. Left
471	      // alone, ⌥⌘S pops that column open: truly empty (`Color.clear.frame(width: 0)`), which is the
472	      // "opens the sidebar as a thinner bar, with nothing in it" bug (issue #128). Catching it here
473	      // and consuming the event stops it from ever reaching AppKit's responder chain; since users
474	      // expect ⌥⌘S to mean "toggle the sidebar" regardless of which one, map it onto our real

514	  /// Stop run commands gracefully on SIGTERM, then exit. macOS routes only a real ⌘Q / Quit
515	  /// Apple-event through `applicationShouldTerminate`, NOT a signal — so without this, a `kill`,
516	  /// `pkill`, or `make app-run` replacing the dev instance would skip the graceful stop and orphan
517	  /// the dev server (a PTY hangup Puma ignores → "A server is already running" later, issue #7). A
518	  /// `DispatchSource` handler runs on the main queue, so it can safely touch the store (a raw signal
519	  /// handler can't); `SIG_IGN` disables the default terminate so the source receives it instead. We
520	  /// `exit()` rather than `NSApp.terminate` to avoid re-entering the quit confirmation, and only
521	  /// after the run commands are gone — the OS then reclaims libghostty as on any quit. SIGKILL /
522	  /// force-quit still can't be caught by anything.
523	  private func installSigtermHandler() {
524	    signal(SIGTERM, SIG_IGN)
525	    let source = DispatchSource.makeSignalSource(signal: SIGTERM, queue: .main)
526	    source.setEventHandler {
527	      // The source fires on the main queue, so we're main-actor-isolated in practice (same pattern
528	      // as the NSEvent monitor above) — assert it so we can touch the store synchronously.
529	      MainActor.assumeIsolated {
530	        // SIGTERM is the path `XCUIApplication.terminate()`, `make app-run` and `pkill` take —
531	        // `applicationShouldTerminate` never runs for a signal, so the session flush has to happen
532	        // here too or none of those exits save anything (issue #46). Same reasoning covers
533	        // persistent sessions: this path skips `stopRunCommandsThenTerminate` entirely, so without
534	        // repeating its persistence-off cleanup here, a `make app-run` relaunch during development
535	        // would leak the previous instance's daemon-held shells exactly like a real quit would.
536	        SessionCoordinator.shared.flushAndFreeze()
537	        let group = DispatchGroup()
538	        if !Defaults[.backgroundSessions] {
539	          group.enter()
540	          Task {
541	            await PersistentSessionService.shared.endAllSessions()
542	            group.leave()
543	          }
544	        }
545	        // A tab closed moments before this signal fires an unstructured kill Task; without
546	        // waiting for it here too, quitting fast enough after a close leaves that one session
547	        // running despite the explicit close, regardless of the persistence setting.
548	        group.enter()
549	        Task {
550	          for store in WindowRegistry.shared.allStores {
551	            await store.terminals.awaitPendingCloseKills()
552	          }
553	          group.leave()
554	        }
555	        group.enter()
556	        WindowRegistry.shared.gracefullyStopAllWindows(timeout: 4) { group.leave() }
557	        group.notify(queue: .main) { exit(EXIT_SUCCESS) }
558	      }
559	    }
560	    source.resume()
561	    sigtermSource = source
562	  }

604	  /// same `openTerminal` path as an in-app panel tap, so there's one routing implementation.

616	        let registry = WindowRegistry.shared
617	        let store = tabID.flatMap { registry.ownerOf(tabID: $0) } ?? registry.keyStore
618	        store?.hostWindow?.makeKeyAndOrderFront(nil)

626	  /// Confirm before quitting unless the user turned it off (`confirmOnQuit`, default on): quitting
627	  /// tears down every terminal (and anything running in them) at once, with no undo. The dialog's
628	  /// "Don't ask me again" checkbox turns the setting off (same key as the menu/Settings toggles).
629	  /// `@MainActor` so the `NSAlert` (a main-actor AppKit type) call is clean — AppKit always invokes
630	  /// this on the main thread. Closing a window doesn't quit the app, so this fires only on a quit.
631	  @MainActor
632	  func applicationShouldTerminate(_ sender: NSApplication) -> NSApplication.TerminateReply {
633	    // UI-test fixture quits cleanly (no modal, no waiting) so XCUITest teardown never blocks. The
634	    // session still flushes here: this branch IS terminating, and a UI test that relaunches to check
635	    // what was restored must not race the coalescing timer (issue #46).
636	    if UITestFixture.isActive {
637	      SessionCoordinator.shared.flushAndFreeze()
638	      return .terminateNow
639	    }
640	    if Defaults[.confirmOnQuit] {
641	      let alert = NSAlert()
642	      alert.messageText = "Quit Workroom?"
643	      alert.informativeText =
644	        Defaults[.backgroundSessions]
645	        ? "Quitting leaves terminals running in the background. They'll be waiting when you reopen Workroom, but any running dev servers will still stop."
646	        : "Quitting closes all terminals and stops any running processes."
647	      alert.addButton(withTitle: "Quit")
648	      alert.addButton(withTitle: "Cancel")
649	      alert.showsSuppressionButton = true
650	      alert.suppressionButton?.title = "Don't ask me again"
651	      let shouldQuit = alert.runModal() == .alertFirstButtonReturn
652	      // Ticking the box stops future confirmations — whether they Quit or Cancel, the checkbox
653	      // means "stop asking". Writes the same key the menu/Settings toggles bind to.
654	      if alert.suppressionButton?.state == .on {
655	        Defaults[.confirmOnQuit] = false
656	      }
657	      guard shouldQuit else { return .terminateCancel }
658	    }
659	    return stopRunCommandsThenTerminate(sender)
660	  }

662	  /// Ctrl-C any live run commands and let them exit before the process dies, so dev servers clean up
663	  /// (release their port + pidfile) instead of being orphaned by the OS hangup on exit — a SIGHUP
664	  /// that Puma ignores, surfacing as "A server is already running" on the next launch (issue #7).
665	  /// Sends only key events — never frees a surface — so the no-mass-free-on-quit rationale in
666	  /// `applicationWillTerminate` still holds. Bounded so a wedged server can't block the quit.
667	  @MainActor
668	  private func stopRunCommandsThenTerminate(_ sender: NSApplication) -> NSApplication.TerminateReply
669	  {
670	    let registry = WindowRegistry.shared
671	    // Mark the app as terminating so a window's own close handler doesn't also prompt/stop (#70).
672	    registry.isTerminating = true
673	    // Write the session and stop writing (issue #46). Deliberately HERE and not at the top of
674	    // `applicationShouldTerminate`: that method can still return `.terminateCancel` at the confirm
675	    // dialog, and freezing above that guard would silently kill session saving for the rest of the
676	    // app's life after one cancelled ⌘Q. This point is past the guard and still before any window
677	    // closes — which is exactly what the freeze protects, since the document is rebuilt from the
678	    // live windows.
679	    SessionCoordinator.shared.flushAndFreeze()
680	    // With persistence off, the daemon does NOT get torn down by quitting (unlike an in-process
681	    // PTY, which the OS SIGHUPs when libghostty's memory is reclaimed — see the doc comment on
682	    // `applicationWillTerminate`): a daemon-held shell is a separate, independent process that
683	    // outlives Workroom on purpose. Nothing else ever kills it once the setting is off, so without
684	    // this every ordinary terminal's session would leak forever — silently contradicting the quit
685	    // alert's own promise ("stops any running processes") the moment the preference is off.
686	    let shouldStopPersistentSessions = !Defaults[.backgroundSessions]
687	    let group = DispatchGroup()
688	    if shouldStopPersistentSessions {
689	      group.enter()
690	      Task {
691	        await PersistentSessionService.shared.endAllSessions()
692	        group.leave()
693	      }
694	    }
695	    // A tab closed moments before quitting fires an unstructured kill Task (`closeTab`); wait for
696	    // it too, unconditionally — the persistence setting and run-command state above don't cover it,
697	    // so skipping this (the old early-return did, when neither applied) let that one session
698	    // outlive the quit despite the user having explicitly closed it.
699	    group.enter()
700	    Task {
701	      for store in registry.allStores { await store.terminals.awaitPendingCloseKills() }
702	      group.leave()
703	    }
704	    if registry.hasAnyLiveRunCommand {
705	      group.enter()
706	      // Stop every window's run commands, not just the focused one's.
707	      registry.gracefullyStopAllWindows(timeout: 5) { group.leave() }
708	    }
709	    group.notify(queue: .main) { sender.reply(toApplicationShouldTerminate: true) }
710	    return .terminateLater
711	  }

713	  /// Reactivation (Dock click, or clicking a notification while the app is inactive): bring an
714	  /// EXISTING window forward rather than letting AppKit open a brand-new one (issue #70). A
715	  /// value-based `WindowGroup` otherwise spawns a fresh window on reopen — so a notification click
716	  /// would pop a new window instead of returning to the window where the event happened (the
717	  /// notification handler then brings that specific owner window forward). Only ask AppKit to create
718	  /// a window when none exists.
719	  func applicationShouldHandleReopen(_ sender: NSApplication, hasVisibleWindows flag: Bool)
720	    -> Bool
721	  {
722	    let registry = WindowRegistry.shared
723	    if let window = registry.lastActiveStore?.hostWindow ?? registry.allStores.first?.hostWindow {
724	      window.makeKeyAndOrderFront(nil)
725	      return false
726	    }
727	    return true
728	  }

730	  /// Deliberately does NOT tear down libghostty on quit. Freeing surfaces (or the app) while their
731	  /// IO/render is still active races libghostty's surface teardown and crashes — EXC_BAD_ACCESS in
732	  /// `Surface.deinit`, or `os_unfair_lock` corruption in `Surface.handleMessage` — most readily when a
733	  /// run command's dev server (issue #7) is still busy. The process is exiting anyway: the OS reclaims
734	  /// libghostty's memory and closes the PTYs, so every child shell/server gets SIGHUP exactly as a
735	  /// manual `ghostty_surface_free` would deliver. (The per-workroom delete path still reaps a single
736	  /// steady-state surface — that's not a mass-free racing termination.)
737	  ///
738	  /// Run commands are the exception that SIGHUP doesn't safely cover: a dev server like Puma ignores
739	  /// the hangup and is left orphaned on its port/pidfile. So `applicationShouldTerminate` Ctrl-Cs
740	  /// every live run command and waits for it to exit *before* returning — sending key events only,
741	  /// never freeing a surface, so the no-mass-free rationale above still holds (issue #7, Option B).
742	  @MainActor
743	  func applicationWillTerminate(_ notification: Notification) {}
744	}

# First-run onboarding wizard (issue #151)

## Context

Issue [#151](https://github.com/joelmoss/workroom/issues/151): "Need a great looking startup intro
and flow for first time usage." The issue body is a single sentence with no further spec.

Research confirms nothing like this exists today: no first-run flag, no welcome window. A brand-new
install currently just shows `ProjectSidebar`'s empty-project `ContentUnavailableView` with an "Add
Project…" button — functional, not an "intro."

Scope was narrowed with the user via Q&A:
- A **4-step wizard** (Welcome → Feature tour → Add Project → Done), not a single sheet.
- Triggers on **first launch ever, only while zero projects are registered** — one-shot, but if
  closed before finishing, it shows again next launch.
- Presented in a **dedicated onboarding window** (its own SwiftUI `Scene`, like `Settings`), not a
  sheet over the main window.
- The existing `ProjectSidebar` empty state stays untouched as the fallback for anyone who
  dismisses/skips the wizard early.

## Design decisions from verified research

- **Reuse, don't rebuild, the Add Project step.** `AddProjectSheet` (`Views/AddProjectSheet.swift`)
  is already a pure, sheet-independent view — `init(onAdd: (String, Bool) -> Void, onCancel: () ->
  Void)` — with its own tested model (`AddProjectSheetModel`, covered by
  `AddProjectSheetModelTests.swift`). The wizard embeds it directly as its 3rd step; no fork, no
  duplicated validation.
- **Drive the real launch-window store, not a throwaway one.** `AppStore.addProject(_:create:)`
  (`Core/AppStore.swift:2983-2999`) does more than register a path — after `reload()` it selects the
  new project (issue #104). A throwaway `AppStore` built just for the onboarding window would apply
  that selection to a store nobody's looking at, leaving the real window's sidebar showing the new
  project with nothing selected. Fix: the wizard's Add-Project step calls
  `WindowRegistry.shared.lastActiveStore?.addProject(...)` — by construction the launch `RootWindow`
  is already registered (and thus `lastActiveStore` non-nil) before the wizard's `.task` can open it.
- **No new `WindowRegistry` registration for the onboarding window.** Leaving it unregistered is what
  makes every existing aux-window carve-out (⌘W fallback, shortcut/switcher no-ops, quit/window-count
  logic, ⌘\` cycle exclusion) apply for free — verified these all key off `WindowRegistry.store(for:)
  == nil`, exactly like Settings/About today. No new code needed in any of those paths.
- **Theming**: read `ThemeService.shared.tokens.*` directly (the actual pattern `WhatsNewSheet`/
  `SettingsView` use — not `@Environment`, despite a stray doc comment suggesting otherwise).
- **No new pager dependency.** No `TabView(.page…)`/carousel exists anywhere in the app; `.page`
  style is iOS-primary anyway. A plain step-`switch` + a small dot-indicator `HStack` is enough for a
  fixed 4-step linear flow.

## Implementation

### 1. New Defaults key — `Core/DefaultsKeys.swift`

Add next to `lastSeenVersion` (same "unset = first launch" shape):

```swift
/// Whether the first-launch onboarding wizard (issue #151) has been completed. Unset (false) on a
/// fresh install. Flips true when the wizard reaches "Done", or when its Add Project step
/// successfully adds a project. The show-gate (`OnboardingGate.shouldShow`) also checks
/// `projects.isEmpty`, so a project added some other way suppresses the wizard too — this flag only
/// needs writing from the wizard itself, not from `AppStore.addProject`'s general path.
static let hasCompletedOnboarding = Key<Bool>("onboarding.hasCompleted", default: false)
```

### 2. New file — `Views/OnboardingWindow.swift`

- `enum OnboardingStep: Int, CaseIterable { case welcome, tour, addProject, done }` — drives which
  step view is shown.
- `enum OnboardingGate { static func shouldShow(hasCompleted: Bool, projectsEmpty: Bool, override:
  Bool? = UITestFixture.onboardingOverride) -> Bool }` — pure, unit-testable (mirrors
  `AddProjectSheetModel`'s "pure logic beside its view" pattern). `!hasCompleted && projectsEmpty`,
  with `override` short-circuiting for UI tests.
- `struct OnboardingFeature: Identifiable` + `static let all: [OnboardingFeature]` — 3-4 cards for the
  tour step, copy grounded in the app's real shipped features (workrooms via Git worktrees/JJ
  workspaces, the embedded terminal, the unified project sidebar, run-command supervision).
- `struct OnboardingWindow: View` — the Scene's root view:
  - `@State private var step: OnboardingStep = .welcome`, `@Environment(\.dismissWindow)`.
  - `body`: `VStack { content; Divider(); footer }.frame(width: 560, height: 480)` (fixed-size, same
    technique as `SettingsView`/`WhatsNewSheet` — no `.windowResizability` needed).
  - `content`: switches on `step` — `.welcome`/`.tour` are new small step views; `.addProject` embeds
    `AddProjectSheet(onAdd:onCancel:)` directly; `.done` is a "You're all set" screen with a "Get
    Started" button.
  - `footer`: Back (steps after `.tour`, except `.addProject` which has its own Cancel/Add buttons),
    step-dot indicator, Next (on `.welcome`/`.tour`).
  - `handleAdd(_:create:)`: resolves `WindowRegistry.shared.lastActiveStore`, calls
    `store.addProject(path, create: create)`, checks `store.errorMessage` — on success, set
    `Defaults[.hasCompletedOnboarding] = true` and advance to `.done`; on failure, leave the step up
    so the user can retry (mirrors how the sidebar's own Add Project flow surfaces errors).
  - `finish()`: sets the Defaults flag, calls `dismissWindow(id: OnboardingWindow.sceneID)`.
  - No `WindowAccessor`/`WindowRegistry.register` call anywhere in this view — that omission is the
    load-bearing part of the aux-window integration (see design decisions above).

### 3. Scene wiring — `WorkroomApp.swift`

Add a `Window` scene (macOS 13+, fine at this app's macOS 15+ floor) in `WorkroomApp.body`, alongside
`Settings`:

```swift
Window("Welcome to Workroom", id: OnboardingWindow.sceneID) {
  OnboardingWindow()
}
```

In `RootWindow.body`'s existing `.task` (`WorkroomApp.swift:155-174`), right after `await
store.bootstrap(restore: seed.restore)` and the `guard seed.isLaunch else { return }`, before the
session-restore fan-out loop:

```swift
if OnboardingGate.shouldShow(
  hasCompleted: Defaults[.hasCompletedOnboarding], projectsEmpty: store.projects.isEmpty
) {
  openWindow(id: OnboardingWindow.sceneID)
}
```

Uses the `@Environment(\.openWindow)` already declared on `RootWindow` (`WorkroomApp.swift:122`).
Gating on `seed.isLaunch` (already required to reach this point in the `.task`) is exactly what stops
onboarding from being reconsidered on a ⌘N window — only the launch window's `.task` body reaches
this line at all.

### 4. UI-test fixture support — `Core/UITestFixture.swift`

- Add `static var onboardingOverride: Bool?` reading a plain string launch arg
  (`-WorkroomUITestOnboarding show|hide`) via the existing `text(_:)` helper — independent of
  `isActive`, like `forceWhatsNew`, so it also covers the non-fixture bootstrap path used by
  `WorkroomWorkflowUITests.testAppLaunchesWithChrome`. (Note: this is a separate string-typed flag
  read directly by application code, not a `Defaults`-typed bool read from a bare launch arg — so it
  does not hit the argument-domain-shadowing gotcha that a naive `-hasCompletedOnboarding 1` arg
  would.)
- In `applyFixtureDefaults(active:)`, pin `Defaults[.hasCompletedOnboarding] = true` alongside the
  existing `sidebarWidth`/`diffViewMode`/`themeFamily` determinism pins — otherwise a machine with a
  clean Dev Defaults domain and `-WorkroomUITestNoProjects 1` (used by e.g.
  `NewWorkroomDialogUITests`) would unexpectedly pop the wizard over an unrelated test.
- Fix `WorkroomWorkflowUITests.swift`'s `testAppLaunchesWithChrome` launch args to include
  `-WorkroomUITestOnboarding hide` (it runs with `fixture: false` against real config/Defaults, so
  the fixture pin above doesn't cover it).
- New `WorkroomAppUITests/OnboardingUITests.swift`: launches with `-WorkroomUITestFixture 1
  -WorkroomUITestNoProjects 1 -WorkroomUITestOnboarding show -ApplePersistenceIgnoreState YES`;
  asserts the window (accessibility id `onboarding.window`) appears, walks Next → Next → Cancel
  (skip) → Get Started, asserts it closes. A second test drives the real Add Project button and
  asserts auto-advance to Done.

### 5. Unit tests — new `WorkroomAppTests/OnboardingGateTests.swift`

Pure calls to `OnboardingGate.shouldShow(hasCompleted:projectsEmpty:override:)` (mirrors
`AddProjectSheetModelTests`): all 4 `(hasCompleted, projectsEmpty)` combinations, plus `override`
forcing true/false regardless of the other params.

No changes to `AppStoreAddProjectTests.swift` — `AppStore.addProject` itself is untouched.

## Files touched

- `macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/DefaultsKeys.swift` — new key.
- `macapp/WorkroomApp/Views/OnboardingWindow.swift` — new.
- `macapp/WorkroomApp/WorkroomApp.swift` — new `Window` scene + `.task` gate/open call.
- `macapp/WorkroomApp/Core/UITestFixture.swift` — override + fixture pin.
- `macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/WorkroomWorkflowUITests.swift` — one launch-arg fix.
- `macapp/WorkroomAppUITests/OnboardingUITests.swift` — new.
- `macapp/WorkroomAppTests/OnboardingGateTests.swift` — new.

New source file needs `make app-generate` (or any `make app-*` build target, which run it
automatically) to be picked up by Xcode.

## Verification

1. `make cli-lint`/`make app-lint` and `make app-format` on touched files.
2. `make app-test` (unit) — `OnboardingGateTests` plus full regression.
3. `make app-generate && xcodebuild ... -only-testing:WorkroomAppUITests/OnboardingUITests` (scoped,
   per the memory on never running the full UI suite) — verify the wizard's UI test, plus a scoped
   rerun of `NewWorkroomDialogUITests`/`WorkroomWorkflowUITests` to confirm the fixture pin/launch-arg
   fix actually prevents the regression it targets.
4. Manual end-to-end, with **two** isolation layers (config is $HOME-scoped; Defaults is not):
   ```bash
   export HOME="$(mktemp -d)"
   defaults delete com.developwithstyle.workroom.dev onboarding.hasCompleted 2>/dev/null
   make app-run
   ```
   Verify: wizard opens over the empty main window on first launch; Next/Next walks Welcome → Tour;
   on Add Project, either add a real project (auto-advances to Done, main sidebar shows it selected)
   or Cancel (also advances to Done, as a skip); Get Started closes the wizard; relaunching does not
   reopen it. Then repeat, closing the wizard early (⌘W before reaching Done) and confirm it *does*
   reopen next launch.
